sample_unit: deidentified asynchronous text-based medical consultation records

links.outcome: Potentially adverse-outcome rate of chatbot vs physician responses in medical decision-making
links.effect: 3.12% (59/1893) of chatbot responses potentially leading to adverse outcomes vs 2.01% (38/1893) for physicians; lower accuracy (96.88% vs 97.99%, P<.001) in decision-making scenario.
links.quote: Errors in chatbot responses were primarily due to misinterpretations of medical terminology or the lack of updated guidelines, with 3.12% (59/1893) of its responses potentially leading to adverse outcomes, compared with 2.01% (38/1893) for physicians.

links.outcome: Chatbot accuracy, safety and trustworthiness by message scenario (education vs decision-making)
links.effect: Education: higher completeness (97.34% vs 93.61%, P=.002), no accuracy/safety difference. Decision-making: lower accuracy and trustworthiness (50.71% vs 93.29% moderately trustworthy or higher, P<.001).
links.quote: In the medical decision-making scenario (n=1893), the chatbot exhibited lower accuracy (n=1834, 96.88% vs n=1855, 97.99% for fully accurate responses; P<.001) and trustworthiness (n=860, 50.71% vs n=1766, 93.29% rated as "Moderately trustworthy" or higher; P<.001) compared with physicians.

unlisted_practices: Comparing patient panel versus clinician panel ratings of AI empathy in message responses

screen.reason: The study retrospectively evaluates GPT-4 responses to real patient messages compared to physician responses, evaluated by both oncologists and patients, but does not test a specific deployment practice or guardrail.
